title: 5 Ways to Recognize Your Blind Spots
paragraphs: 5 Ways to Recognize Your Blind Spots
The things destroying you rarely announce themselves.
There is a frightening possibility that most people never seriously consider.
What if the greatest threat to your spiritual life is not the sin you know about?
What if it is the sin you cannot see?
Not the struggle you confess.
Not the weakness you battle.
Not the temptation that keeps you awake at night.
But the hidden flaw that quietly shapes your decisions, poisons your relationships, hardens your heart, and distances you from God while convincing you everything is fine.
That is the danger of a blind spot.
A blind spot is not merely ignorance.
It is unseen reality.
It is truth standing directly in front of you while remaining invisible to you.
The most dangerous blind spots are not the ones others refuse to talk about.
They are the ones everyone sees except you.
The Pharisees had them.
King David had them.
Peter had them.
The churches in Revelation had them.
And if Scripture is honest about anything, it is this:
So do we.
David cried out in Psalm 19:12:
"Who can discern his errors? Forgive my hidden faults."
The Hebrew is breathtaking.
The phrase "hidden faults" comes from the Hebrew word:
נִסְתָּרוֹת (nistarot)
Meaning:
"things concealed, hidden things, secret matters, things beyond one's awareness."
David was not merely asking forgiveness for known sins.
He was asking forgiveness for sins he could not even see.
That should humble every believer alive.
Because if a man after God's own heart feared hidden faults...
Perhaps we should too.
The terrifying reality is that blind spots often grow in the soil of sincerity.
You can genuinely love God and still be deceived.
You can serve faithfully and still be blind.
You can know Scripture and still miss what God is trying to show you.
That is why recognizing blind spots is not optional.
It is survival.
The first way to recognize a blind spot is when you constantly explain why everyone else is wrong.
Some people spend years building court cases against everyone around them.
Every failed relationship was someone else's fault.
Every conflict was caused by another person.
Every criticism was unfair.
Every correction was misunderstood.
Eventually a pattern emerges.
The common denominator is not everyone else.
It is you.
Proverbs 12:15 says:
"The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice."
The Hebrew word for fool here is:
אֱוִיל (ewil)
Not someone lacking intelligence.
Someone who rejects correction.
Someone who assumes they are already right.
Blind spots often reveal themselves through defensiveness.
When correction feels like an attack instead of an opportunity, something deeper may be happening beneath the surface.
The second way to recognize a blind spot is when you become uncomfortable around truth-tellers.
Nathan walked into David's palace and shattered an illusion.
David had convinced himself he was still the righteous king.
Nathan exposed the hidden corruption.
At first David could see the sin clearly.
Just not his own.
Then Nathan spoke the words that changed history:
"You are the man."
Suddenly blindness became sight.
Repentance became possible.
Restoration began.
Many people claim they want truth.
Few actually want exposure.
Yet Scripture teaches that faithful wounds from a friend can save a soul.
If every honest voice eventually gets pushed out of your life, your blind spots will become stronger than your convictions.
The third way to recognize a blind spot is when your public image matters more than your private reality.
Jesus repeatedly confronted religious leaders who looked holy while hiding corruption underneath.
In Matthew 23:27 He said:
"Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs."
The Greek word for hypocrite is:
ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs)
Originally referring to a stage actor.
Someone performing a role.
Someone presenting an image.
Someone wearing a mask.
The danger was never merely that the Pharisees sinned.
The danger was that they became experts at appearing righteous.
Blind spots thrive wherever image management replaces genuine transformation.
God is not impressed by spiritual performance.
He is after surrendered hearts.
Many people spend years polishing the outside while neglecting the inside.
But heaven sees both.
The fourth way to recognize a blind spot is when recurring pain keeps appearing in different places.
Different job.
Same conflict.
Different church.
Same offense.
Different relationship.
Same wounds.
Different season.
Same struggle.
At some point wisdom asks a difficult question:
What if the problem is not merely around me?
What if part of it is within me?
This is not about self-condemnation.
It is about self-awareness.
The Holy Spirit does not reveal blind spots to shame us.
He reveals them to heal us.
Jesus said in John 16:13 that the Spirit would guide believers into truth.
Notice He did not say comfortable truth.
He said truth.
Sometimes healing begins where excuses end.
The fifth way to recognize a blind spot is when prayer becomes one-sided.
Many prayers are conversations where we do all the talking.
We bring requests.
Needs.
Frustrations.
Desires.
Plans.
But rarely pause long enough for God to expose what we do not see.
One of the most dangerous prayers is also one of the most powerful.
David prayed:
"Search me, O God."
The Hebrew word for search is:
חָקַר (chaqar)
Meaning:
"to investigate thoroughly, examine deeply, explore completely."
David invited divine examination.
Not partial inspection.
Not surface-level review.
Complete exposure.
Most people ask God for blessing.
David asked God for scrutiny.
Because he understood something many believers forget:
God cannot heal what we refuse to uncover.
The irony of blind spots is that once they are revealed, they often seem obvious.
Peter insisted he would never deny Christ.
Hours later he did exactly what he swore was impossible.
The church in Laodicea believed they were rich.
Jesus said they were poor.
Samson believed he was strong.
His strength had already departed.
Blindness always feels like sight until truth arrives.
That is why humility is one of the greatest spiritual protections God gives His people.
Humility keeps learning.
Humility keeps listening.
Humility keeps repenting.
Humility keeps growing.
The proud assume they have arrived.
The humble know God still has work to do.
Perhaps that is why the most mature believers often speak the least about their own greatness.
The closer they get to God, the more clearly they see themselves.
And the more clearly they see themselves, the more deeply they cling to grace.
Maybe while reading this, a face came to mind.
A conversation.
A wound.
A habit.
A pattern.
A conviction.
Something uncomfortable.
Something familiar.
Something you've been avoiding.
Do not ignore that moment.
The Holy Spirit often whispers before He shouts.
And sometimes the breakthrough you've been praying for is hidden behind the blind spot you've been protecting.
Be honest.
Which of these five areas exposed something in your own life?
Someone you know desperately needs this message.
One day you will thank God for every truth that wounded your pride but saved your soul.
